title: How staff orchestras worked
summary: Radio staff orchestras and union scale changes.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: Well, I went into -- see, I left Benny Goodman in 1943 and I went into CBS, what they called the staff orchestra which was -- you know, in those days it was just radio and they had what they called staff orchestras. That

was when the orchestra would play for time that had not been sold commercially. The union gave them a special weekly price which was lower than commercial scale. But on the other hand, a station could not put on any commercial programs. If one of their what they called pilot programs, if they got sold to a sponsor, then the staff musicians wouldn't do it and they had to hire outside musicians and pay them a higher scale. Of course, the staff musicians could be hired but they would still have to be paid outside scale. It only was after television came in that they started allowing the staff orchestras to play commercial programs. But the networks more or less made a move and took over commercial programs from the agencies. At one time those were only handled by agencies and the networks just sold the time to the agencies and they had no part in the production of the programs.

But little by little they sort of pushed the agencies out of that field and took it over themselves. So I think that by 1958, I think, when I was on the Como show, National Broadcasting Company then paid the musicians instead of Perry Como, and Perry Como paid the National Broadcasting Company a lump sum for the time and everything else. They furnished the musicians, the camera crew and so forth. So that used to be in the hands of the stars, all the networks did was just sell them time. They weren't involved in any other way.
